body: Now,
Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont is proposing a nationwide moratorium on construction of new data centers.
It's a temporary pause, not an outright ban. He has said that he wishes to give democracy a chance to catch up with "the transformative changes that we are witnessing."
Neighborhood concerns are legitimate, and Sanders has positioned himself as a moderate voice on the subject. But
a moratorium is a bad idea
— even a temporary one.
Data centers are positive contributors to local, regional and national economies,
even if they do not directly employ large numbers of people once they are operational.
They directly impact our economy.
Their slowdown will spark catastrophic chain reactions.
Global AI development and digital economy expansion is today
bottlenecked by the speed of data center development,
further slowdowns will reverse all existing economic expansion agendas.

The organization that I head, the International Data Center Authority (IDCA), takes a worldwide view of data center development. Our research shows a strong correlation between the creation of data center hubs and strong local economies.
Data centers are indeed
the foundation of all business and personal computers,
mobile phones, and valued services such as Netflix, Instagram and other social media, online shopping and convenient government services.
The clearest example is the world's largest data center hub in Loudoun County, Va., outside Washington, D.C.
Loudoun County has been transformed from one of the poorest to one of the richest local economies in the U.S.

due to its data center-driven economy. Hundreds of data centers have reshaped the county from an undistinguished rural region into an economic powerhouse that delivers more than $1 billion annually to local schools and supports one of the highest per capita income regions in the world.

Concerns about providing sufficient future power for new centers there have led to a six-year waiting period for new projects. Even so, the Loudoun County economic development office continues to receive applications for new projects (i.e. investments).

As far as land, many data centers are renovating large, old and abandoned sites that have sat as toxic eyesores for years. The Homer City Energy Campus east of Pittsburgh will operate on the site of what was the largest coal-fired utility in Pennsylvania.

Meta is operating two new data centers on former textile manufacturing sites in North Carolina, with EPA approval. A Texas company recently announced plans to renovate an abandoned paper mill site into a new data center, halfway between Dallas and Houston.

All these projects vastly increase the value of the land in their areas. In Loudoun County, a recent transaction encompassing more than 100 acres sold for more than $6 million per acre. Data centers are bringing this new prosperity to economic zones worldwide.

As for water and noise, the massive new AI centers often propose the use of closed-loop cooling, meaning they don't draw on the rumored immense local water resources once in operation. New designs and operating methods are also obviating the noise that older-style centers once created.
